options.text: TLS has been configured correctly for Hubble, because the option that would disable it is set to false.
TLS is currently disabled for Hubble and must be switched on before any further validation can take place.
The value is a placeholder written by the Hubble CLI pod, which has not yet been created in the cluster.
Hubble Relay is running, but the Hubble server certificate has expired and must be renewed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to verify the configuration before beginning, and states that you should see the `hubble-disable-tls` configuration option set to `false`. A value of `false` therefore means TLS is not being disabled, that is, it has been configured correctly, and you can continue with the validation procedure.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the meaning of the flag: `false` means TLS is not disabled, so it is not a signal that TLS must be switched on.

questions.stem: You run two clusters joined by Cluster Mesh. A global Service named rebel-base already exists, and in cluster 1 you run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=local --overwrite`. You then curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1 while healthy backends exist in both clusters. What do you observe?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only, because the local backends are preferred while they remain healthy.
The replies come from pods in both clusters, because a global Service always balances across every cluster.
The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only, because the annotation pushes traffic away from the local cluster.
No replies arrive until the annotation is removed, because the local preference blocks remote endpoints permanently.

questions.explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to local makes the Global Service prefer healthy backends in the local cluster. Remote endpoints are used only as a fallback, so a client in cluster 1 keeps being served by cluster 1 pods for as long as those backends are available and healthy.

optionRationale.b: This is the behaviour without any affinity preference; the local value deliberately overrides it while local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: That is the effect of the remote value, not the local value.
optionRationale.d: Remote endpoints are not blocked permanently; they are used if and only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy.

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only.
The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only.
The replies come from pods in both clusters as usual.
The request fails, because a cluster cannot prefer endpoints it does not host.

questions.explanation: Switching the annotation to remote inverts the preference: the endpoints of the other cluster become the preferred destination, so a client in cluster 1 is served by cluster 2 pods.

optionRationale.b: That is what the local value produces, not the remote value.
optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour with no affinity preference, or when the client sits in the cluster that is not the preferred one.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the request succeeding and being answered by cluster 2 pods.

questions.stem: A global Service carries no `service.cilium.io/affinity` annotation at all. What preference does Cilium apply?

options.text: None — there is no preference, which is the default behaviour when the annotation does not exist.
Local — endpoints in the local cluster are preferred whenever they are available.
Remote — endpoints in remote clusters are preferred whenever they are available.
Global — the service is balanced strictly across all clusters with no local endpoints considered.

questions.explanation: The annotation accepts none, local and remote. The value none is the default and means no preference, and it is also the behaviour applied when the annotation is absent altogether.

optionRationale.b: Local is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.c: Remote is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.d: Global is not one of the listed values for this annotation; the global behaviour comes from the separate service.cilium.io/global annotation.

questions.stem: An engineer runs Cilium 1.16 with the Gateway API enabled and switches on host network mode, because no LoadBalancer Service is available in the development cluster. One Gateway listener is configured on port 8080 and a TCPRoute is attached to that Gateway. What should the engineer expect to happen to the TCPRoute traffic?

options.text: It bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which is now a NodePort Service using a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than port 8080.
It is proxied through Envoy and served on port 8080 on all host interfaces, exactly as configured on the listener.
Host network mode is refused and the Gateway remains in LoadBalancer Service mode until the TCPRoute is removed.
It is served on port 8080, but only on the loopback interface, because host network mode binds listeners to 0.0.0.0.

questions.explanation: Host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly. That Service would normally expose the configured Gateway listener port as a LoadBalancer Service, but enabling host network mode turns it into a NodePort Service, which receives a randomly assigned port from the node port range instead of the port configured on the listener. The engineer should therefore not assume that port 8080 is the port actually serving the TCPRoute traffic.

optionRationale.b: This describes the normal Envoy-proxied path on the configured listener port, but TCPRoute and UDPRoute traffic bypasses Envoy under host network mode and the generated Service becomes a NodePort Service with a random port.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute, not that enabling it is refused; the mode is enabled and the Service type changes instead.
optionRationale.d: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6), not on the loopback interface, and the port is not the configured listener port for these route types.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling host network mode turns this Service into a ``NodePort`` Service instead, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the ``Gateway`` listener.

questions.stem: You apply a `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` that denies all traffic by default, then run `curl --fail -v http://"$HTTP_INGRESS"/details/1` against the Cilium Ingress. According to the excerpt, what happens?

options.text: The request is denied: curl reports HTTP 403 Forbidden, and the Hubble flow shows the HTTP request DROPPED with a 403 response FORWARDED.
The request succeeds with HTTP 200 OK because the default-deny policy applies only to in-cluster traffic, not to external traffic arriving through the Ingress.
The request is denied with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable because Envoy cannot reach any backend once the policy is applied.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so curl reports a connection timeout rather than an HTTP status code.

questions.explanation: With the default-deny `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` applied, the excerpt states that the request to the `/details` endpoint is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The curl output shows `HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden` with `server: envoy`, and the Hubble observe output shows the `http-request DROPPED` followed by an `http-response FORWARDED` carrying the 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the request is denied for external and in-cluster traffic, so external traffic through the Ingress is not exempt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden response, not a 503 Service Unavailable.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows an HTTP 403 response being returned, not a TCP-level connection timeout.

citations.title: Default Deny Ingress Policy
citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium Gateway API behind a trusted cloud load balancer. The load balancer injects an `X-Forwarded-For` header containing the original client IP. The team wants Cilium's Layer 7 policies, including Ingress, to be applied using that client IP rather than the address of the load balancer connection. Which configuration change matches the Cilium documentation?

options.text: Set `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` section of the values files.
Set the trusted hop count to `1` so Envoy uses the rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` value for policy decisions.
Set `useRemoteAddress` to `true` so Envoy trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header.
Do nothing, because Envoy already uses `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that when you trust the traffic source to inject an `X-Forwarded-For` header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header by setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` sections of values files. The trusted-hop count changes how Envoy derives the visible source address for `X-Forwarded-For`, and `X-Envoy-External-Address` is a header Envoy sets; neither is the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the `X-Forwarded-For` client IP.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the trusted-hop count as controlling which `X-Forwarded-For` value Envoy uses for the visible source address, not as the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt specifies setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false`, not `true`, to force Envoy to treat traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Envoy sets `X-Envoy-External-Address` to the trusted client address, but it does not say that this header is already used as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster has WireGuard transparent encryption enabled. Two pods that are both scheduled on the same node exchange traffic with each other, and an engineer watching the node's traffic expects to see that traffic protected by the WireGuard tunnel. What does Cilium actually do with these packets?

options.text: It leaves them unencrypted, because traffic destined to the same node it was sent from is deliberately not encrypted.
It encrypts them, because WireGuard is enabled cluster-wide for every Cilium-managed endpoint.
It encrypts them only when the two pods belong to different namespaces.
It drops them unless a CiliumNetworkPolicy explicitly allows pod-to-pod traffic on that node.

questions.explanation: WireGuard encryption in Cilium covers traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes. When the source and the destination are the same node, the packets are not encrypted, and the excerpt states that this behaviour is intended: the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway, so encryption would provide no benefit.

optionRationale.b: Enabling WireGuard does not encrypt every packet; the same-node case is explicitly excluded from encryption.
optionRationale.c: Namespace membership plays no part in the decision — the criterion given is whether the traffic is destined to the node it was sent from.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about dropping same-node traffic; it says such packets are simply not encrypted.

citations.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
citations.quote:
Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which
they were sent. This behavior is intended.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a Cilium cluster whose nodes are spread across several routing domains, and the routers in the underlying network have no knowledge of the cluster's PodCIDRs. According to the excerpt, what does the encapsulation model require of that underlying network?

options.text: The underlying network must be configured with the PodCIDRs so that its routers can forward pod traffic.
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant, provided the cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.
All cluster nodes must sit within a single link-layer domain for encapsulated traffic to flow.
The PodCIDR size must be chosen to fit within the addressing limitations of the underlying network.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists simplicity as an advantage of the model: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs, and cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains. The only requirement stated is reachability between nodes using IP/UDP, which makes the underlying topology irrelevant. Options a, c and d each contradict a specific statement in the excerpt.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains, so a single link-layer domain is not required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the addressing space does not depend on any underlying networking limitations, so the PodCIDR need not be fitted to them.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant as long as
  cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.stem: In Cilium's encapsulation model, what purpose does the excerpt give for carrying the source security identity as metadata in the network packet?

options.text: It encrypts the packet payload between the cluster nodes.
It is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.
It lets the remote node learn the PodCIDR of the sending node.
It removes the need for cluster nodes to reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that encapsulation protocols allow metadata to be carried along with the network packet, and that Cilium uses this to transfer metadata such as the source security identity. It then states that this identity transfer is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node. The other options describe functions the excerpt does not attribute to the identity transfer.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes metadata transfer for the source security identity, not encryption of the payload.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link the identity transfer to PodCIDR discovery; it concerns the source security identity.
optionRationale.d: Node reachability over IP/UDP is described separately as a property of the model, not as something the identity transfer removes.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The identity transfer is an optimization
  designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.

questions.stem: An operator holds CAP_SYS_ADMIN in their own current user namespace and uses pod exec to enter a running Cilium agent container. Under what condition does this amount to privileged access?

options.text: Only if CAP_SYS_ADMIN is also held in the Cilium user namespace, which is the initial namespace.
Only if the operator also holds CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the Cilium container.
Always, because the Linux kernel permits joining other namespaces by default.
Only if the Cilium agent's volumes were mounted with unsafe options.

questions.explanation: The kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, so entering the Cilium container requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the current user namespace and the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace). When both namespaces carry that capability, the access is already privileged. Holding CAP_NET_ADMIN, kernel defaults or volume mount options play no part in this test.

optionRationale.b: CAP_NET_ADMIN is not the capability named in the excerpt; the test is CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so mount options are not the deciding factor.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: To enter the Cilium container, the ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN`` capability is required in both the current user namespace and in the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace).

questions.stem: Why does the Cilium agent need kernel interfaces that cannot be virtualized or namespaced?

options.text: Because some kernel interfaces are part of the /proc filesystem, which includes host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.
Because Cilium mounts host volumes with unsafe options that bypass namespaces.
Because the Cilium agent runs without any Linux capabilities at all.
Because Kubernetes does not support user namespaces on cluster nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that Cilium needs kernel interfaces to configure the environment properly, and that some of these interfaces sit in the /proc filesystem, which carries host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced. The remaining options contradict the excerpt, which says Cilium needs specific Linux capabilities and performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says Cilium doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt opens by stating the Cilium agent needs some specific Linux capabilities.
optionRationale.d: User namespace support is not discussed; the limitation given is about /proc contents, not Kubernetes support.

questions.stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that contains two ingress rules. The first rule matches a broad set of traffic, and the second matches a narrower set that overlaps with the first. A colleague is concerned that the narrower rule will somehow cut down what the broader rule permits. How does Cilium treat traffic that matches either of the two rules?

options.text: It is allowed, because the rules are additive: traffic matching the union of the rules is permitted.
It is allowed only if it matches the narrower rule, because the more specific rule takes precedence over the broader one.
It is allowed only where the two rules do not overlap, because intersecting rules cancel each other out.
It is allowed only if it matches both rules at once, because the rules in a policy are combined with a logical AND.

questions.explanation: Cilium policy rules follow a whitelist model: each rule allows the traffic that matches it, and rules are additive rather than subtractive. Where two rules overlap, the traffic matching the union of those rules is allowed, so adding a narrower rule alongside a broader one does not remove anything the broader rule already permitted. The colleague's concern is therefore unfounded. Note that traffic which matches none of the rules is dropped pursuant to the `policy_enforcement_modes`.

optionRationale.b: There is no precedence for a more specific rule in the whitelist model; a narrower rule simply adds its own matches to those of the broader rule rather than overriding it.
optionRationale.c: Rules do not cancel one another out on overlap; the excerpt states that traffic matching the union of intersecting rules is allowed.
optionRationale.d: Rules are not combined with a logical AND requiring a match against every rule; each rule independently allows the traffic that matches it.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote: If there is an intersection between two or more rules, then traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that includes a `toPorts` entry with both an `http` rule list and a `dns` rule list for the same port. What is the outcome?

options.text: The policy is rejected, because mixing different port level rule types in a single port is disallowed.

The policy is accepted but the port is treated as having no layer 7 rules.

questions.explanation: The `L7Rules` structure is a union: exactly one of the protocol-specific fields must be set per port, and mixing different port level rule types is disallowed. Supplying both `http` and `dns` for the same port therefore makes the policy invalid.

optionRationale.b: The union design forbids combining members on one port, so they are not both applied in any order.
optionRationale.c: Silently dropping one member is not what the excerpt describes; mixing is disallowed outright.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that if none are specified no additional port level rules apply, but here two conflicting types are specified, which is a rejection case.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes combining or rejecting, not first-match discarding.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selection with identical `PortProtocol` triggers the combine-or-reject rule, so they are not treated independently.

questions.stem: You have created a single VNet peering from cluster one's virtual network to cluster two's virtual network using `az network vnet peering create` with `--allow-vnet-access`. What connectivity does this give you?

options.text: Outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two only; the reverse direction needs a second peering.
Full bi-directional traffic, because a single peering is always symmetric.
No traffic at all until a route table is attached to both virtual networks.
Only traffic between the control planes, not node-to-node traffic.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the first peering command allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two, and that bi-directional traffic requires adding a peering in the other direction as well.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says virtual networks can't connect by default and that bi-directional traffic requires a peering in the other direction too, so one peering is not symmetric.
optionRationale.c: No route table is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the peering itself is what enables cross-VNet communication.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no distinction between control-plane and node traffic; it speaks of outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks

This allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two. To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

questions.stem: An engineer has run the peering command from cluster one to cluster two and now wants node-to-node traffic between the clusters to work in both directions. What must be done next according to the excerpt?

options.text: Add a peering from cluster two to cluster one, using cluster one's VNet ID as the remote VNet.

Delete the first peering, since two peerings on the same pair of VNets conflict.
Nothing further; node-to-node traffic is already possible after the first peering.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never suggests removing `--allow-vnet-access`; both example commands include it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say the first peering must be deleted; it says to add a peering to the other direction as well.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says node-to-node traffic is possible only after the second, reverse peering is added.

bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

questions.stem: In the excerpt's first peering command, how is the remote virtual network supplied to `az network vnet peering create`?

Via `--vnet-name`, which is set to the remote cluster's network name.
Via `--resource-group`, which points at the remote cluster's resource group.
Via `--name`, which is set to the remote peering's name.

questions.stem: An engineer is validating addressing before enabling Cluster Mesh. Which requirement does the excerpt place on PodCIDR ranges?

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium with metrics enabled but has left `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` at `false`. They want Prometheus to discover the Cilium metrics endpoints without a ServiceMonitor. What does the chart provide for this?

optionRationale.c: The headless service the chart creates is named `cilium-agent`, and it exists to collect Envoy metrics, not operator metrics.

optionRationale.c: The opposite is true: the excerpt says traditional approaches filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says eBPF works transparently without requiring the application to change in any way; it does not attribute an application-modification requirement to iptables.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium Cluster Mesh across three clusters. One remote cluster's connection drops and is not restored. An engineer wants Cilium to stop sending global-service traffic to that cluster's backends after a defined period, rather than continuing to use cached information. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero, such as `"15m"`.
Leave `clustermesh.cacheTTL` at its default of `"0s"`, which revokes caches after the built-in grace period.
Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to `"0s"` to force immediate revocation of cached data.
Disable global services on the unreachable cluster so its backends are removed from the cache.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that to mitigate stale backends you can configure a cache TTL, and that to enable it you set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero (e.g., `"15m"`). With a non-zero TTL, if the connection is lost and not re-established within that duration, Cilium revokes the cached data and stops load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's global-service backends.

optionRationale.b: The default ``"0s"`` disables the feature and means caches are never revoked, so no grace-period revocation occurs.
optionRationale.c: ``"0s"`` is the default that disables the feature; it does not force immediate revocation.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes configuring a cache TTL, not disabling global services on the remote cluster.

optionRationale.c: ``"15m"`` is given only as an example of a value greater than zero, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such distinction; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.

With `"0s"` caches are revoked immediately, whereas a duration greater than zero delays revocation until the connection is re-established.
With `"0s"` only global-service caches are revoked, whereas a duration greater than zero revokes all cached data.
With `"0s"` caches are revoked after fifteen minutes, whereas a duration greater than zero disables revocation.

optionRationale.b: ``"0s"`` does not revoke immediately; it disables revocation entirely.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt draws no distinction by service type; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.
optionRationale.d: The roles are reversed: ``"0s"`` disables the feature, and ``"15m"`` is an example of an enabling value.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation to let backends reply directly to external clients without the extra hop, and also wants policy at the backend node to be able to match on the client's source IP. Which change achieves both goals?

questions.explanation: Setting loadBalancer.mode to dsr makes Cilium operate in DSR mode, in which backends reply directly to the external client without the extra hop and the client's source IP is preserved so policy can match on it at the backend node.

optionRationale.b: That flag disables the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554; it has nothing to do with DSR or source IP preservation.
optionRationale.c: SNAT mode is precisely the mode in which the client's source IP is not preserved, so keeping it cannot meet the requirement.
optionRationale.d: Disabling address checking may be necessary for DSR to work in some clouds, but it does not itself switch Cilium into DSR mode.

questions.stem: An operator is tuning a Cilium deployment and wants to avoid the MTU reduction that DSR would otherwise require for UDP traffic, while still using DSR for TCP. What does the excerpt say makes this possible?

options.text: For TCP services, Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, not subsequent ones, which allows a hybrid mode using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Cilium encodes the service IP/port in every TCP packet, so the MTU reduction applies equally to TCP and UDP.
The loadBalancer.mode option accepts a per-protocol value that selects DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Setting bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true removes the need for any MTU reduction.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the stated optimisation, which limits encoding to the SYN packet for TCP.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the hybrid mode as an optimisation arising from SYN-only encoding, not as a per-protocol value of loadBalancer.mode.
optionRationale.d: That flag relates to the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554, not to MTU reduction for DSR.

questions.stem: An operator has set both `spec.eni.subnet-ids` and `spec.eni.subnet-tags` on the CiliumNode. A new ENI must be allocated. How are the candidate subnets determined?

questions.stem: The Cilium Operator becomes temporarily unavailable in a cluster. According to the excerpt, what is the expected effect?

optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions agents declaring kvstore unhealthiness and restarting as a consequence of a stale heartbeat key, not an immediate restart of every agent with removal of eBPF programs.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, how does the socket operations hook differ in what it is attached to and what it reacts to, compared with the socket send/recv hook?

optionRationale.d: The `--protocol http` output contains the `tiefighter` request and response, so allowed traffic is observed.

`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator`
`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`
`spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and they want the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. After enabling host network mode via Helm, what happens to the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode?

options.text: It is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
It remains active and both modes serve traffic simultaneously on different ports.
It is converted into a shared Ingress listener on port 8080.
It is left untouched but must be disabled manually before host network mode takes effect.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No manual step is required, and the modes cannot run together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both serve traffic at once.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes converting the Service mode into a shared listener; the Service mode is simply disabled.
optionRationale.d: The disabling is automatic, not a manual prerequisite.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress host listener port annotation. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The annotation is mandatory in this situation, so the Ingress resource must set ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.
The Ingress resource silently falls back to the shared listener on port 8080.
The Ingress resource inherits the port from ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort.
The Ingress resource is rejected only if the global mode is shared rather than dedicated.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory if the global mode is configured to dedicated, or if the Ingress resource sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the annotation as mandatory in this case, not as having a silent fallback.
optionRationale.c: The sharedListenerPort Helm flag belongs to the shared Ingress method, not to the dedicated per-Ingress annotation.
optionRationale.d: The mandatory condition applies when the global mode is dedicated, which is the opposite of what this option claims.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

questions.stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy, and the backend application must see the original client IP. Which Service setting does the excerpt say is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this situation?

options.text: Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` on the Service.
Leave `externalTrafficPolicy` unset so that Kubernetes defaults it to `Local`.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and disable the `healthCheckNodePort`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that with `Local`, nodes route only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, and that in clusters using `kube-proxy` this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

optionRationale.b: ``Cluster`` is described as allowing the node to masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that leaving the field unset defaults it to ``Local``; it only describes the two relevant settings.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``healthCheckNodePort`` is automatically set by Kubernetes when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, and does not suggest disabling it.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
Because of this, in clusters that use
  ``kube-proxy``, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

questions.stem: In a setup where Istio ambient mode with mTLS and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are in use, which component should enforce policy for traffic between Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads at L4 or above?

options.text: Istio.
Cilium, using its L7 HTTP policy controls.
Cilium, using Kubernetes NetworkPolicy at L7.
Both Cilium and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Because Cilium cannot see the source, destination or L7 details of the tunneled and encrypted traffic, the excerpt concludes that Istio should be used to enforce policy for traffic between Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads at L4 or above.

optionRationale.b: Cilium has no visibility into any L7 information for that tunneled and encrypted traffic.
optionRationale.c: Cilium-enforced Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is described as applying to traffic ingressing from non-Istio-managed workloads, not to the mTLS-secured inter-workload traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not recommend using both Cilium and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls at the same time, to avoid split-brain problems.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote: This means that Istio should be used to enforce policy for traffic between Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads at L4 or above.

optionRationale.c: 10.0.1.0/24 is used in the excerpt as the CIDR block for Cluster_1_Public_Subnet_1, not as a VPC range to avoid.

questions.stem: An engineer has just added service.cilium.io/shared="false" to the rebel-base Service in cluster 1. Before removing the annotation, they run kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should they observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in both clusters.
Replies only from pods in cluster 1.
Replies only from pods in cluster 2.
No replies from any pods.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that, after the annotation is added in cluster 1, accessing the global service from cluster 1 still shows replies from pods in both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 1.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that replies are still seen from pods in both clusters, not that no pods reply.

questions.stem: A policy contains two `toPorts` entries. Both entries use the same `PortProtocol` and select an overlapping list of endpoints. The first entry defines HTTP layer 7 rules, while the second defines DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The policy is rejected because the layer 7 rule types differ.
The HTTP and DNS rules are combined and both are enforced.
The HTTP rules are kept and the DNS rules are silently ignored.
The DNS rules are kept and the HTTP rules are silently ignored.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that layer 7 rules from multiple `toPorts` entries with the same `PortProtocol` and overlapping endpoints are combined only when they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.b: Combining is permitted only when the layer 7 rules are of the same type; here the types differ.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

questions.stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints and also a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules for the same endpoints. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion of the second rule?

options.text: It has no effect.
It is enforced in addition to the first layer 4 rule.
It overrides the first layer 4 rule and permits only matching layer 7 requests.
It causes the policy to be rejected because layer 4 and layer 7 rules cannot coexist.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when a layer 4 rule is specified and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, the layer 7 portions of the latter rule have no effect.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the layer 7 portions have no effect, not that they are enforced in addition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe the layer 7 portion overriding the first layer 4 rule.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the policy is rejected; it says the layer 7 portions have no effect.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy, and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the latter rule will have no effect.

questions.stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy has been applied that whitelists traffic sent from any pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. A tiefighter pod carrying the label org=empire sends a POST request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds and returns Ship landed.
The request is blocked because the policy matches endpoint IP addresses rather than pod labels.
The request hangs because Cilium connection tracking permits only reply packets, not the initial request.
The request succeeds only if the xwing pod is also labelled org=empire.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the policy whitelists traffic from pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. It then says that only the tiefighter pods with the label org=empire will succeed, while the xwing pods will be blocked. Therefore the tiefighter request succeeds and returns Ship landed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies; matching is by pod labels.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes stateful connection tracking as automatically allowing required reply packets; it does not say the initial request is blocked.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says xwing pods will be blocked; the tiefighter request succeeds because the source pod has org=empire, not because xwing is labelled.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed. The *xwing* pods will be blocked!

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for pods that may be rescheduled to different nodes. They are deciding whether to select the pods by endpoint IP address or by pod label. What does the excerpt say they should do?

options.text: Use endpoint IP addresses, because they remain stable when pods are rescheduled.
Use the labels assigned to the pods, because endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant and policies are applied based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running.
Use the deathstar service DNS name, because Cilium policies match on service names rather than pod identity.
Use both endpoint IP addresses and pod labels, because Cilium requires an IP address in every policy rule.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies and that labels assigned to pods should be used instead. It adds that policies are applied to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running within the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies, not stable selection keys.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt discusses pod labels and endpoint IP addresses; it does not say policies match on service DNS names.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use labels instead of endpoint IP addresses; it does not require both.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy

questions.stem: An engineer is preparing the second peering command, the one that creates the peering from cluster two to cluster one. Before running az network vnet peering create, the engineer must populate the VNET_ID variable. Which value does the excerpt assign to VNET_ID for this command?

options.text: The ID of cluster one's virtual network, queried from the resource group "${CLUSTER1}-group" and the virtual network "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net".
The ID of cluster two's virtual network, queried from the resource group "${CLUSTER2}-group" and the virtual network "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net".
The name of cluster one's virtual network rather than its ID, taken from the --name argument.
The name of cluster one's resource group, taken from the --resource-group argument.

questions.explanation: In the second command block the VNET_ID variable is populated by querying the virtual network in "${CLUSTER1}-group" named "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net", and that value is then passed to --remote-vnet when the peering is created in "${CLUSTER2}-group". The remote virtual network for the reverse peering is therefore cluster one's virtual network.

optionRationale.b: Cluster two's virtual network is the one the peering is created in (--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"); it is not the remote virtual network referenced by VNET_ID in this block.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt queries the ID with --query id -o tsv, so the variable holds the ID rather than the name.
optionRationale.d: The resource group is used to locate the virtual network in the az network vnet show command; the value assigned to VNET_ID is the virtual network's ID.

questions.stem: A platform team has installed Cilium with the host firewall enabled and applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector to select a group of worker nodes. On one of those selected nodes, two workloads send traffic to destinations outside the cluster: pod A runs with hostNetwork: true, while pod B runs in its own pod network namespace. How does the host policy treat these two flows?

options.text: Both flows are covered, because the policy selects the node on which both pods are running.
Pod A's traffic is covered, because host policies apply to the host namespace including host-networking pods; pod B's traffic to a location outside the cluster is not covered.
Neither flow is covered, because host policies apply only to the node's own host namespace and never to any pod.
Only pod B's traffic is covered, because host policies explicitly exclude host-networking pods from the host namespace.

questions.explanation: A host policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector, and it applies to all the nodes that selector picks. Within each selected node, however, its scope is the host namespace, which expressly includes host-networking pods. Communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster fall outside that scope, so pod B's flow is not governed by the host policy even though its node is selected.

optionRationale.a: Selecting the node is necessary but not sufficient: the policy's scope inside the node is the host namespace, so a pod in its own network namespace sending traffic outside the cluster is not covered.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host policies apply to the host namespace 'including host-networking pods', so host-networking pod traffic is covered rather than excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: host-networking pods are included in the host namespace, and it is non-host-networking pods talking to locations outside the cluster that are excluded.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote: Host policies apply to all the nodes selected by their NodeSelector. In each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including host-networking pods. They don't apply to communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: An engineer has a LoadBalancer Service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges populated. By default the CIDR restrictions apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. The engineer wants those CIDRs to filter traffic for all externally exposed service types as well. Which action does the excerpt describe for this?

options.text: Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true in Helm.
Add the annotation service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer to the Service.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny.
Remove spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges so that no restrictions are applied.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that by default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service. It then states that propagating the white-listed CIDRs to all externally exposed service types can be enabled in Helm via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.

optionRationale.b: The service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer annotation is described as a way to avoid the creation of corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not as a way to propagate the CIDRs to them.
optionRationale.c: Setting service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not propagate the list to the other service types.
optionRationale.d: Removing spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges would leave the field empty, and the excerpt says that if the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: This option can be enabled in Helm via ``bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true``.

questions.stem: A platform team is rolling out Cilium on a new cluster and wants Pod-level rate limiting in place from the start. What is the default state of the bandwidth manager on a fresh installation, and what must they do?

options.text: It is enabled by default, so no action is needed beyond annotating Pods.
It is disabled by default on new installations, so Cilium must be installed with the bandwidth manager enabled.
It is enabled by default only when BPF Host Routing is also enabled.
It is disabled by default and can only be turned on by chaining the bandwidth CNI plugin.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations, and that to install Cilium with it enabled you must install Cilium with the bandwidth manager enabled. Nothing in the excerpt makes it conditional on BPF Host Routing, and the bandwidth manager explicitly does not use CNI chaining.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: it is disabled by default on new installations.
optionRationale.c: BPF Host Routing is strongly recommended as a companion, but the excerpt does not make the default enablement conditional on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: Cilium's bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations.

questions.stem: Which statement about the scope of Cilium's bandwidth enforcement and its relationship to BBR congestion control matches the excerpt?

options.text: Enforcement works only in tunneling mode, and BBR requires the bandwidth CNI plugin.
Enforcement works only in direct routing mode, and BBR is unrelated to the bandwidth manager.
Enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode, and the bandwidth manager is a prerequisite for enabling BBR congestion control for Pods.
Enforcement requires CNI chaining, and BBR is enabled automatically once annotations are present.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode in Cilium, and that Cilium's bandwidth manager is also prerequisite for enabling BBR congestion control for Pods.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt supports both modes and does not tie BBR to the CNI plugin.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt supports both direct routing and tunneling, and it explicitly links the bandwidth manager to BBR.
optionRationale.d: The bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining, and the excerpt does not say BBR is enabled automatically by annotations.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling
mode in Cilium.

questions.stem: A Pod carries both the `kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth` and `kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth` annotations. According to the excerpt, how is each of these limits enforced?

options.text: Egress is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT, while ingress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.
Both egress and ingress are enforced using EDT at the native host networking devices.
Both egress and ingress are enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.
Egress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation, while ingress is enforced at the native host networking devices using EDT.

questions.explanation: The excerpt distinguishes the two directions: the `egress-bandwidth` is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the `ingress-bandwidth` is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation. The other options either merge the two mechanisms or swap them between directions.

optionRationale.b: EDT is described as the mechanism for egress only; ingress uses an eBPF-based token bucket.
optionRationale.c: The eBPF-based token bucket is described as the mechanism for ingress only; egress uses EDT.
optionRationale.d: The mechanisms are reversed: EDT applies to egress and the token bucket to ingress.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The ``egress-bandwidth`` is enforced on egress at
the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ``ingress-bandwidth``
is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

questions.stem: After enabling encryption, the Cilium Pods fail to start. Which two things should you first double-check according to the troubleshooting guidance?

options.text: That the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together
That the IPsec Secret is deployed in the kube-system namespace while Cilium runs in its own namespace
That the encryption interface has been set with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`
That `cilium-dbg encrypt status` reports a non-zero error counter

questions.explanation: The excerpt's first troubleshooting step for Cilium Pods that fail to start after enabling encryption is to double-check whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt requires the Secret and Cilium to be in the same namespace; it does not name kube-system or describe separate namespaces.
optionRationale.c: Setting the encryption interface is the remedy for a `Device eth0 does not exist` warning in the logs, not the first check for Pods failing to start.
optionRationale.d: Running `cilium-dbg encrypt status` is a later diagnostic step, and a non-zero error counter relates to kernel XFRM errors, not to Pods failing to start.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if
   the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

questions.stem: An engineer is told that only one of the two optional methods for enabling cilium-health monitoring needs to be permitted by the firewall. Which pair of methods does the excerpt describe?

options.text: ICMP Type 0/8, Code 0 among all nodes, or TCP 4240 among all nodes.
TCP 4240 among all nodes, or UDP 51871 among all nodes.
ICMP Type 0/8, Code 0 among all nodes, or UDP 8472 among all nodes.
TCP 4244 among all nodes, or TCP 4245 among all nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt recommends, but does not require, that all nodes be able to ping each other (ICMP Type 0/8, Code 0) and that TCP 4240 be open among all nodes for cilium-health monitoring, and notes that only one of these two methods may be used.

optionRationale.b: UDP 51871 is the WireGuard port, not a health-monitoring method.
optionRationale.c: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port, not a health-monitoring method.
optionRationale.d: TCP 4244 and 4245 are the Hubble server and Hubble Relay ports, not health-monitoring methods.

citations.title: Firewall Rules

questions.stem: An engineer is comparing the overlay modes described in the excerpt. Which statement correctly pairs each mode with its port?

options.text: VXLAN uses UDP 8472 and Geneve uses UDP 6081.
VXLAN uses UDP 6081 and Geneve uses UDP 8472.
VXLAN uses UDP 51871 and Geneve uses UDP 8472.
VXLAN uses TCP 8472 and Geneve uses TCP 6081.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two ports; the excerpt assigns 8472 to VXLAN and 6081 to Geneve.
optionRationale.c: UDP 51871 is the WireGuard port, not the VXLAN port.
optionRationale.d: Both overlay ports are described as UDP, not TCP.

citations.title: Firewall Rules

The same
applies to Geneve overlay network mode, except the port is UDP 6081.

questions.stem: An engineer in cluster 1 changes the annotation on the existing global service `rebel-base` to `service.cilium.io/affinity=remote` and then curls the service from cluster 1. What is the result?

options.text: Replies come from pods in cluster 2 only.
Replies come from pods in cluster 1 only.
Replies come from pods in both clusters as usual.
The service stops resolving until the annotation is removed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt's step 6 states that after changing the annotation to `remote`, accessing the global service from cluster 1 produces replies from pods in cluster 2 only.

optionRationale.b: Replies from cluster 1 only is the outcome of the `local` value, not `remote`.
optionRationale.c: Replies from both clusters as usual is what happens with no affinity preference, or when accessing from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the service still responding, just from the other cluster's pods.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: This time, the replies are coming from pods in ``cluster 2`` only.

questions.stem: What is the default behaviour when the `service.cilium.io/affinity` annotation does not exist on a global service?

options.text: No preference; the default behaviour applies.
Local endpoints are preferred.

questions.stem: You run the fortio load test against `http://echo-service:8080` with `-c 2 -qps 0 -n 20`. The run completes and the summary reports `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. According to the excerpt, what does the presence of that 503 indicate?

options.text: It triggers a circuit breaker.
It shows that the fortio Pod could not resolve the Service name.
It proves that all 20 requests failed to reach the backend.
It indicates that the load generator ran out of sockets.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the 503 response code seen in the output triggers a circuit breaker. Only a single request returned 503, so the run was not a total failure, and nothing in the excerpt attributes the 503 to DNS resolution or socket exhaustion.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the name resolved to 10.96.182.43:8080, so resolution was not the problem, and it never links 503 to DNS.
optionRationale.c: The summary shows 19 of 20 requests returned 200, so the vast majority succeeded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt reports `Sockets used: 3 (for perfect keepalive, would be 2)` without attributing the 503 to socket exhaustion.

questions.stem: You want to raise the load on `http://echo-service:8080` from the two concurrent connections used in the first run. Which fortio invocation does the excerpt use to bring the number of concurrent connections up to 4?

options.text: `kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 4 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080`
`kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 40 http://echo-service:8080`
`kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 4 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080`
`kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 20 -qps 0 -n 4 http://echo-service:8080`

questions.explanation: The excerpt raises concurrency by changing the `-c` flag from 2 to 4 while keeping `-qps 0` and `-n 20`, which is the command it shows for bringing the number of concurrent connections up to 4.

optionRationale.b: This keeps two concurrent connections and instead doubles the request count to 40, which is not what the excerpt does.
optionRationale.c: This keeps `-c 2` and sets a non-zero qps, which does not raise the connection count to 4.
optionRationale.d: This swaps the values of `-c` and `-n`, giving 20 connections and 4 requests, which is not the command shown.

questions.stem: Before running the load test, the excerpt sets up an environment variable holding the fortio Pod name. Which command does it use to populate `FORTIO_POD`?

options.text: `export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=fortio -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')`
`export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get svc -l app=fortio -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')`
`export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=echo-service -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].metadata.name}')`
`export FORTIO_POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=fortio -o 'jsonpath={.items[0].spec.containers[0].name}')`

questions.explanation: The excerpt builds the variable from a Pod listing filtered by `app=fortio` and extracts the first item's `metadata.name`, which is the Pod name.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt queries pods, not services, so listing `svc` is wrong.
optionRationale.c: The label selector in the excerpt is `app=fortio`, not `app=echo-service`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt extracts `metadata.name`, not the container name from the spec.

questions.stem: You are preparing the second EKS cluster for Cluster Mesh and are about to create its VPC. A colleague suggests using 172.17.0.0/16 as the CIDR block. What does the guide advise, and why?

options.text: Avoid 172.17.0.0/16, because certain AWS services utilise this range and using it could cause potential issues.
Use 172.17.0.0/16, because it is the range reserved for Cluster Mesh inter-cluster traffic.
Avoid 10.1.0.0/16, because certain AWS services utilise this range and using it could cause potential issues.
Any CIDR is acceptable, because the VPC CIDR is overridden by the Cluster Mesh pod CIDR.

questions.explanation: The guide explicitly warns against the 172.17.0.0/16 range for the VPC, stating that certain AWS services utilise this range, so using it could cause potential issues. The example VPC for cluster two is instead created with 10.1.0.0/16.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no indication that 172.17.0.0/16 is reserved for Cluster Mesh traffic; it is named as a range to avoid.
optionRationale.c: The warning concerns 172.17.0.0/16, not 10.1.0.0/16, which is the CIDR block used in the example create-vpc command.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the VPC CIDR is overridden by a pod CIDR; it gives a specific warning about which range to avoid.

Cluster_2_Private_Subnet_1 and Cluster_2_Private_Subnet_2

questions.stem: You run `kubectl get gateway -A` and see a Gateway in namespace `website` whose CLASS column shows `cilium`, but the PROGRAMMED column is empty. According to the excerpt, what should you check first?

options.text: Make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.
Make sure that a LoadBalancer implementation is present, because the gateway has no address.
Make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed, because the resource type was not found.
Make sure the Gateway's class is changed to `cilium`, since Cilium only programs Gateways with that class.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that a programmed Gateway means Cilium prepared a configuration for it, and that if the `Programmed true` indicator is missing you should make sure Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration. The class is already `cilium` here, so the class check does not apply, and the resource was clearly found because it appears in the output.

optionRationale.b: A missing address is a separate check in the excerpt, tied to whether a LoadBalancer service is assigned; the question concerns the missing Programmed indicator, not the address.
optionRationale.c: The CRD check applies when the Gateway API resource type is not found, but here the Gateway is listed in the output.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium only programs Gateways with the class `cilium`, and the output already shows that class, so no change is needed.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the ``Programmed true`` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.

questions.stem: An engineer enables host network mode and wants the shared HTTP listener to be reachable on a host port different from the shared listener port, while leaving the other shared listeners on the default. Which Helm value should be set?

options.text: ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.tlsPassthroughPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port

questions.explanation: The httpPort value sets the host network port for the shared HTTP listener specifically. If it is unset or 0, the sharedListenerPort value is used instead, which is why the other listeners stay on the default.

optionRationale.a: sharedListenerPort sets the port for the Envoy listener generally and is the fallback for the individual listeners; changing it would move all shared listeners, not just HTTP.
optionRationale.c: tlsPassthroughPort applies to the shared TLS passthrough listener, not the HTTP listener.
optionRationale.d: This is an annotation applied per Ingress resource for dedicated ingress, not a Helm value for the shared HTTP listener.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: ``ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort``: Host network port to expose the shared HTTP listener. If unset or ``0``, ``sharedListenerPort`` is used.

questions.stem: After applying a Cilium-managed L4 network policy restricting the `blue` namespace to clients in `blue` and `red`, the checks behave as expected. You then enhance the policy to a Cilium L7 network policy allowing only the `/ip` URL path. The connectivity checks now show `client 'red' to server 'blue': 503` and `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 503`. What does the excerpt say is the cause, and what must you do to allow Cilium to manage L7 policy?

options.text: The Cilium proxy (HTTP) interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPs connections; you must disable Istio's mTLS authentication by configuring a new policy.
The L4 policy was applied to the wrong namespace; you must reapply it in the `red` namespace.
Istio is in `PERMISSIVE` mode; you must switch it to `STRICT` mode so that mTLS is enforced.
The `/ip` path is not permitted by the Cilium proxy; you must add `/deny` to the allowed paths.

questions.explanation: Once the L7 policy is in place, all communication with the `blue` namespace breaks because the Cilium proxy (HTTP) interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPs connections. The remedy given is to disable Istio's mTLS authentication by configuring a new policy, applied to the same namespace where the HTTP-based network policy is implemented.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not attribute the failure to the policy's namespace placement; it attributes it to the Cilium proxy interfering with Istio's mTLS connections.
optionRationale.c: ``PERMISSIVE`` is the default described earlier and is not presented as the cause of the 503 responses.
optionRationale.d: ``/deny`` is used afterwards to verify that Cilium is enforcing the L7 policy, returning 403; it is not a fix for the 503 responses.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium alongside Istio in ambient mode. They want Cilium L7 HTTP policy to govern traffic for a particular workload, but that workload is currently enrolled in Istio ambient. What must they do so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy on that workload's traffic?

options.text: Remove the workload from Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
Set `mtls.mode=DISABLE` in an Istio PeerAuthentication resource for that workload.
Leave the workload in ambient mode but enable Cilium L7 policy, since Cilium can inspect traffic tunneled over port 15008.
Configure `hostNetwork: true` on the istiod pods so that Cilium can reach the workload's sidecar.

questions.explanation: In ambient mode, the way to make a workload subject to Cilium L7 policy is to take it out of Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`. Otherwise Istio encrypts the traffic with mTLS and Cilium cannot access it for L7 policy enforcement. Disabling mTLS via PeerAuthentication is the sidecar-mode remedy, not the ambient one.

optionRationale.b: ``mtls.mode=DISABLE`` under PeerAuthentication is the instruction given for sidecar mode, not for ambient mode.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that traffic tunneled and encrypted by Istio over port 15008 gives Cilium no visibility into source, destination or any L7 information, so leaving the workload in ambient does not work.
optionRationale.d: ``hostNetwork: true`` on istiod is a requirement for sidecar mode with automatic injection and Cilium overlay mode, unrelated to L7 policy enforcement.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Ambient: Remove the workloads you wish to manage with Cilium L7 policy from Istio ambient by removing either the
    ``istio.io/dataplane-mode`` label from the namespace,
    or annotating the pods you wish to manage with Cilium L7 with ``ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled``.

questions.stem: How does the excerpt contrast the `Local` and `Cluster` settings of `externalTrafficPolicy` for a Loadbalancer or NodePort Service?

options.text: `Local` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, whereas `Cluster` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and the node may masquerade the source IP.
`Local` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, whereas `Cluster` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP.
`Local` routes only to Pods on the local node but always masquerades the source IP, whereas `Cluster` never masquerades the source IP.
`Local` and `Cluster` differ only in the health check port number that Kubernetes assigns automatically.

questions.explanation: The excerpt gives two relevant settings. `Local`: nodes route traffic only to Pods running on the local node, without masquerading the source IP. `Cluster`: the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, which in many cases may mean the backend pod does not see the source IP.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two definitions; the excerpt assigns even cluster-wide routing to `Cluster` and local-only routing to `Local`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says `Local` routes without masquerading the source IP, and that `Cluster` *may* masquerade it, not that it never does.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the `healthCheckNodePort` as automatically set when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set; it does not present port numbering as the difference between the two settings.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
- ``Local``: Nodes will only route traffic to Pods running on the local node, 
  *without masquerading the source IP*.
